language_wrapper: Let b be an integer with b ≥ 2. Call a positive integer n refined b-eautiful if, when written in base b, it has exactly two digits x and y (with x ≥ 1 and 0 ≤ y ≤ b − 1), its digit sum x + y equals √n, it satisfies x + y ≡ {residue} (mod {modulus}), and gcd(x, y) = {gcd_target}. Find the least integer b ≥ 2 for which there are more than {threshold} refined b-eautiful integers.
hardness_rationale: The family retains the core mechanism of the seed—two-digit base-b numbers whose digit sum equals the square root—while adding layered constraints: a modular condition on the digit sum and a coprimality constraint on the digits. Solving requires exploiting the quadratic relation and its discriminant 1 + 4x(b − 1) being a perfect square, then filtering by number-theoretic conditions. The search for the least base with more than a threshold number of valid integers, combined with these filters and a strict threshold, increases both combinatorial and number-theoretic complexity beyond the seed.
notes: Counting relies on the discriminant trick: for each leading digit x, the trailing digit y exists (and is unique in range) iff 1 + 4x(b − 1) is a perfect square with correct parity; this accelerates enumeration substantially. The generator retries to ensure the minimal base is large enough to avoid trivial instances.
source_question: Let $b \geq 2$ be an integer. Call a positive integer $n$ $b\textit{-eautiful}$ if it has exactly two digits when expressed in base $b$ , and these two digits sum to $\sqrt{n}$ . For example, $81$ is $13$ -eautiful because $81=\underline{6}$ $\underline{3}_{13}$ and $6+3=\sqrt{81}$ . Find the least integer $b\geq 2$ for which there are more than ten $b$ -eautiful integers.
